maintopic: CORRUPT PRACTICES AT ELECTIONS BILLS WITHDRAWN

speechtext:
Bill intituled: "An Act to amend the Dominion Controverted Elections Act."- The Solicitor General.
Bill intituled: "An Act to amend the Corrupt Practices Inquiries Act."-The Solicitor General.
Bill intituled: "An Act to amend the Disfranchising Act."-The Solicitor General.
Hon. HUGH GUTHRIE (Acting Solicitor General) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 39, to amend the statutes relating to corrupt practices at elections.

Explain,
please.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this Bill
is intended to take the place of the three Bills which appear on the Order Paper and which at my request have to-day been withdrawn. At first it was thought proper to amend the three separate Acts, namely, the Dominion Controverted Elections Act,-the Corrupt Practices Inquiries Act, and

the Disfranchising Act. The amendments were all consequential amendments, consequent upon the passage of the Act last session known as the Dominion Elections Act. The House will remember that prior to the enactment of the Dominion Elections Act at the last session we had an offence under the former law known as the offence of "corrupting practice" or "corrupt practice". In the law passed past session we added an offence of irregularity, known as an "illegal practice", so that now we have these two irregularities in our layr, the "corrupt practice" and "illegal practice." The Dominion Controverted Elections Act, the Corrupt Practices Inquiries Act, and the Disfranchising Act, were drawn in reference to the law as it formerly stood, and as these Acts appear on the statute book to-day, they take no cognizance whatever of "illegal practices." The Chief Electoral Officer has prepared the Bill which I ask for leave to introduce, to meet this difficulty and to apply as an amendment to the three Acts which I have just specified.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

speechtext:
The House in committee on Bill No. 15, to incorporate the North American Trust Company of Canada, and recommending that the title be changed to "An Act to incorporate the Scottish Canadian Trust Company."-Mr. Mowat.-Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1-incorporation:

maintopic: NORTH AMERICAN TRUST COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
In view of the discussion which took place in the House at the last sitting, when objection was taken by another company, and having regard to

the fact that it is not the desire of the promoters of the Bill to take any undue advantage, I would ask that the matter stand and that the Bill be referred back to the Committee on Banking and Commerce.

But some objection has been made even to the change in name, and it is thought that the Banking and Commerce Committee can better dispose of these differences than they can be disposed of here.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: NORTH AMERICAN TRUST COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Mowat moves
that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.

maintopic: NORTH AMERICAN TRUST COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
Before this motion is adopted I desire to say a few words as chairman of the committee. When the matter came up on Friday last I was in my place and had intended to speak at that time, but it appeared to me that the procedure was not strictly in accordance with the rules of the House, inasmuch as the motion was put when the Speaker was about to leave the Chair. This special Bill should not have been mentioned at that time; the motion usually is that the House go into Committee of the Whole on private bills, no specific bill being mentioned. Now, we have endeavoured in the committee to arrive at satisfactory conclusions on the matters that have come before us. It would be well for this committee to look at rule 91, which refers to this matter and which distinctly states, on page 51, that when an application of this kind is made-
The name of the proposed company shall be stated in the notice.
In this case, we had three names stated in the notice, and at the request of the promoters of the Bill, the change was made from the " North American Company to the Scottish-Canadian Company." During the six weeks that this Bill had been advertised, no objection was taken to the words "Scotish-Canadian." I think the committee will realize that it is very difficult to get a name that does not conflict with the ideas of someone with regard to incorporations. For instance, the word " Empire " occurs five times, and the word

" Canada " probably occurs twenty times in lists of incorporations that have been made within recent years, so that it is difficult to get a name that suits all parties. The desire of the committee is that the name shall be distintive, and as regards the use of the words " Scottish " and " Canadian," if they the used together in any one Act, the name apears to me sufficiently distinctive. But in this particular case, if I am properly informed, though there is a company styled the " Scottish-Canadian," incoporated by an Act of the province of Quebec, that company has not been organized and is not doing business. I could not say definitely as to that, but that is my information. If that be the case, and it does not appear in the records of the House that we have ever granted an incorporation under that name, it would appear to me that it is not taking too much for granted if we allow the name " Scottish-Canadian " to stand. I do not want to take any ground that will jeopardize the rights of any company; as chairman of the committee, I am desirous that we should avoid doing so; but this House has power to fix the name and the committee has not.

maintopic: NORTH AMERICAN TRUST COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
Was any objection
taken to the name while it was advertised?

maintopic: NORTH AMERICAN TRUST COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
No, and the proposed incorporation was advertised for six weeks. Up to the present moment, I have, as chairman of the committee, had no intimation that the name was objected to. The first intimation I had was on Friday last when it was moved, without discussion, that the Bill be referred back, and I had no knowledge of the reasons for that action. We had three names to choose from-North American, Scottish-Canadian and Metropolitan. It is quite possible that the name " Metropolitan " will be objected to, so that the committee will then be powerless to give the Bill a name. It is particularly provided, under the rules of the House, that the final motion is that the Bill be passed and, the title be as in the Order Paper, or some other name which the House is willing should be placed on the Bill. If there is material evidence to offer to the committee with regard to the objection of using the name " Scottish-Canadian," certainly we could have no objection to hearing that; but up to the present, I have had given to me no reason that I think at all sufficient to warrant the referring back of the Bill. I would suggest that the Bill be considered in order to find out if there is anything else to which objection might be taken, and then

if it is thought of sufficient importance by this committee to refer it back, that action might be taken.

maintopic: NORTH AMERICAN TRUST COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext: I have no personal objection to the Bill as it stands, but I might remind hy hon. friend that the three names which have been suggested for this trust company are, to my personal knowledge, already used by insurance companies. I was mentioning1 one a moment ago.

maintopic: NORTH AMERICAN TRUST COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
This is not an insurance company; it is a trust company.
Mr. LEMIEUX I know that, but the names are used by some big insurance companies. The North American Trust suggests the idea that it might be a subsidiary of the North American Life Assurance Company, the Metropolitan Trust suggests the idea that it might be a subsidiary of the Metropolitan Life Insurance Company, and the name " Scottish-Canadian " is, if I am not mistaken, used by the old London and Lancashire Insurance Company of Montreal, which has changed its name to the Scottish-Canadian Insurance Company. I happen to know this through some business which I did not very long ago with that company. I do not at all object if the committee is agreeable to giving that name to the trust company, but I warn my hon. friend that, perhaps, some interested parties might object to it. Perhaps, if we should refer the Bill back to the committee, after Easter it could come before the House again. I have no personal objection; I am only pointing out that all three names are suggestive of three life assurance companies, and my hon. friend, I know would be the last man to injure, even by implication and through a name, any other firm.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: NORTH AMERICAN TRUST COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
I know nothing about this particular case, except that on Friday night last at about five minutes to eight o'clock, the solicitor for the Scottish Canadian Trust Company or Scottish Trust Company of Canada-I do not know exactly which it is-came to me and asked me to request the committee to refer this Bill back in order that further consideration might be given to the name. There is an evident blunder in the name as it appears in the Orders of the Day. It is called the "Scottish Canadian Trust Company of Canada," so that there is an unnecessary duplication, and it would be necessary to refer it back on account of that. The complaint made to me was that when the Bill was originally advertised, it was advertised in the name of the North
American Trust Company. It is true two alternative names were submitted, but any one glancing at the advertisement would think it was the North American Trust Company. It happens there is a Scottish Canadian Insurance Company and a Scottish Trust Company of Canada, both of them having their head office in Quebec. If the name is referred back to the committee the matter can be settled without great difficulty, and those persons who are interested or who think they have a grievance can appear and state their cases.

maintopic: NORTH AMERICAN TRUST COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext: I should like also to say to my hon. friend (Mr. Cockshutt) that, as regards the use of the words "Royal" or "Empire," some years ago, that is, prior to 1911, an Order in Council was passed by the Federal Government at the request of the Home Government that the Canadian Government do hot issue letters patent to or incorporate companies using those names. I know the rule was strictly adhered to, and I do not know how it has happened that since then we have allowed any companies to use the name "Empire" or the name "Royal."

maintopic: NORTH AMERICAN TRUST COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext: I quite recognize the force of the hon. gentleman's argument. I want to point out-I do not think I did so before-that we were limited to those three names, all of which my hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) says will be objected to.

maintopic: NORTH AMERICAN TRUST COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext: They might be.

maintopic: NORTH AMERICAN TRUST COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
I understood my
hon. friend to say that they would be. I am pointing out that, under the rules of the House, it is necessary that the name shall be stated and that it shall be advertised for six weeks. A period of six weeks at this stage of the proceedings is quite a serious item. It would be probably a week or two before the advertisement would appear, so that it might be eight weeks before this Bill could again come before the House, even if we succeeded fairly well in getting a name that is not objected to. The rule is that the name has to be advertised, and we could not violate that rule without special permission.

maintopic: NORTH AMERICAN TRUST COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext: What is the name of the company?

maintopic: NORTH AMERICAN TRUST COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext: At present, as appears on the Order Paper, "The Scottish Canadian Trust Company of Canada."

maintopic: NORTH AMERICAN TRUST COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext: "Where does the word "Royal" come in?

maintopic: NORTH AMERICAN TRUST COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext: It does not come in at all. That word was just mentioned as a precaution, that we should not use it in any alternative name. The words "of Canada" are tautological, and should be struck out. The mover of the amendment did not notice that at the time, and I was going to move that those words be struck out. This committee could do that without referring the Bill back. I want the committee to understand, however, that under the rules, if one or other of these three names is not selected, it will be necessary to have another six weeks' advertising in the Gazette.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: NORTH AMERICAN TRUST COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext: It has been done many times without it.

maintopic: NORTH AMERICAN TRUST COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
May I suggest that the
committee can fix it in a few minutes. You could adopt one of these names. The name, North American Trust Company, does not conflict with the name of any other trust company that I know of.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: NORTH AMERICAN TRUST COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
I might point out to the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cock-shutt) that on Friday evening no motion was made concerning this Bill whatever. When the Order was called for the House to go into Committee of the Whole on this Bill the motion, which will be found on page 112 of the Votes and Proceedings, read as follows:
Mr. Fripp moved, That Mr. Speaker do now leave the Chair for the House to go into Committee of the Whole on Private Bills (pursuant to rule 109) ; which was agreed to.
This Bill was not considered in Committee of the Whole owing to the objection made by the hon. the acting Solicitor General, upon the motion to go into committee. Concerning the request which has now been made that the Bill be referred back to the Select Standing Committee on Banking and Commerce, I must rule that the Committee of the Whole House has no right to make this reference. It will therefore be necessary for this committee to report progress to Mr. Speaker, and a motion made in the House to refer the Bill back to the Banking and Commerce Committee, will then be in order.

maintopic: NORTH AMERICAN TRUST COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
Perhaps I might be pardoned, Mr. Chairman, for drawing your attention to how the matter appears in Hansard, for that is where I was looking. It appears by Hansard that Mr. Fripp moved:
That the House go into 'Committee on Bill No. 15, to incorporate the North American Trust Company of Canada, and recommending that

the title he changed to "An Act to Incorporate the Scottish Canadian Trust Company of Canada."-Mr. Mowatt.
I think the Votes and Proceedings is Correct, and that Hansard is incorrect.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: NORTH AMERICAN TRUST COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
The mistake in Hansard is easily explainable by the fact that the motion was made immediately after the Clerk Assistant had read that order, though it was a different motion that was submitted from the Chair.
Progress reported.

maintopic: NORTH AMERICAN TRUST COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
I beg to move:
That the Order of the Day for the House to go into committee on Bill No. 15, An Act to Incorporate North American Trust Company of Canada, be discharged and that the Bill be referred back to the Select Standing Committee on Banking and Commerce.

subtopic: THE HOUSING PROBLEM. PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF A FEDERAL HOUSING BOARD
speechtext: That, in the opinion of this House, the general interest of the people of Canada will be served by making it possible for every industrious, frugal and thrifty citizen to become the owner in fee simple of a house and lot; that the Government of Canada should grant assistance to make that possible; and to that end, the sum of ten million' dollars should be appropriated annually for a period of five years to buy land and build houses for men of good character who can make a small initial payment and undertake to liquidate the indebtedness incurred by monthly instalments as may be agreed upon; that a Federal Housing Board be appointed to carry out the plan which, for the first year-or such longer period as in the opinion of the Governor General in Council may be desirable-shall be confined to men who have served overseas.

speechtext:
Perhaps I may be permitted
to say a word or two on the point of order. This is a general resolution which undoubtedly involves the spending of money, but in this respect it differs from the resolution to which I took exception the other day, moved by the hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Campbell). I am not going to argue that this resolution is in order, but I would point out that it might be held to be in order, while the other was ruled out of order, for a reason which I shall now advance. There is nothing in this resolution which, if the House saw fit to pass it, would involve a charge at any definite time upon the public treasury. The resolution of the hon. member for Nelson, however, had it carried, would have involved a charge this year on the public treasury. I was not in the House when your Honour's decision was given on that resolution, but it would seem to me that any resolution so reading should be held to be without the powers of a private member of the House. The present resolution is different and I do not wish to apply my argument thereto, but in my judgment it is well worthy of consideration whether it is not also beyond the competence of a private member.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: THE HOUSING PROBLEM. PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF A FEDERAL HOUSING BOARD
speechtext:
The point of order
raises a question which involves a principle affecting to a rather marked degree the rights of private members of the House. In earlier years the practice was to exclude resolutions of this character as being money resolutions, and therefore not competent to be moved by private members. However, in recent years the tendency has grown up to relax the rule and to regard these resolutions, although in their own terms intending to involve the expenditure of money, as being merely an expression of opinion on the part of the hon. member who moves them, or of the House of Commons if the resolution should be adopted. Perhaps I should say also that as far as I can gather the spirit which has prompted speakers heretofore to not regard these resolutions as money resolutions in the
sense that they ought not to be adopted is, that they were to be deemed merely an expression of opinion, and that the Government was not ipso facto to be bound to implement the expression of opinion contained in the resolution. In other words the constitutional rule and duty of the Government to be responsible for initiating financial legislation was not to be impaired in any degree.
As I said the other day my feeling with respect to such resolutions is this: that it seems to be in the highest degree desirable that hon. members should have as much latitude as possible to discuss all manner of questions affecting the public welfare, and that they ought not to be restricted by the application of the rigorous letter of the law. My own tendency is to so interpret the rules of the House as to always permit the widest possible measure of discussion. I shall not give a final opinion at present upon this resolution but will take further opportunity of looking into the matter. I have already indicated what my own view at the moment is, having regard to pi'evious decisions, having regard to previous acts of this House, and having regard to the decision I gave a few days ago -which I may say I found out afterwards was confirmed absolutely by a considered opinion given by Mr. Speaker Sproule in this House a very few years ago, and I may add in connection therewith that it was a judgment reversing a decision of his own of the day before so that it was his matured opinion. At that time he restored to the Order Paper a resolution which on the previous day he had ruled out, a resolution which in its terms called for the expenditure of public money on the part of this House. As at present advised I am inclined therefore to regard this motion as being in order, but I shall take the question into consideration and acquaint the House with my decision in due course.

On the contrary what your Honour has just stated seems to be most reasonable-that private members should have a right to express a pious opinion about public matters. subtopic: THE HOUSING PROBLEM. PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF A FEDERAL HOUSING BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am quite content to amend the resolution in the manner suggested by the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux). I do not think, and I did not think, that I could do much more at this time than ventilate this question in the House. The resolution expresses an opinion that I have had for many years; and the more deeply I have studied this question, the more convinced I have become that the proposal to place every head of a household in this country in possession of his own house and lot is good, sound public policy. I scarcely expected that the Government would have $10,000,000 to appropriate off hand for this purpose, and perhaps I may be accused of having a good deal of assurance in presenting such a suggestion; but I feel satisfied, Mr. Speaker, that that amount of money could not be expended by the Government to better advantage than in the way that I suggest, and I will at least endeavour to show why a broad policy on this question should be adopted.
In the past, Mr. Speaker, the accepted function of a government was to build railways in the West, and wharves in the Maritime Provinces, and, occasionally an armoury building in the province of Ontario. Such will always be an important part of national administration. As the country develops construction must proceed, and I am not arguing that there should be any cessation of expenditures that are necessary for such purposes. But we have reached a time in the history of the world when the common people look for something more from the Government than the construction of roads and public buildings. Some people say that the war has brought this about. My judgment is that it was coming years before the war; it may have been accelerated by the great conflict but was not caused by it. Slowly, during the past generations, a conviction has been growing in the minds of the common people that the needs of the masses demand more attention from those who administer the affairs of the nation. The first manifestation of this is to be found in muni-

cipal government, as far as my experience goes. Fifteen years ago there was a great awakening, Mr. Speaker, among the thoughtful men and women as to the responsibility upon the part of government for the amelioration of the conditions of life among the least fortunate portion of the community. We find this exhibited in the new method adopted in all progressive states and provinces for the treatment of those who have been incarcerated in prisons for violations, of the law. Not so long ago the one idea in handling criminals was their punishment; to-day the dominant idea in dealing with them is to bring about their reformation. I mention this as one of the outstanding developments of a more intelligent study of human needs that distinguishes this generation. I might follov) it in many directions, because the same spirit is displayed in dealing with defectives of all kinds, and in providng for those who lack opportunities for self-development, physically, mentally and morally. The underlying motive of all this is the betterment of the people

the betterment of the common people, and by that term I mean the great majority of our population who must always be employed as wage earners. Those who have the organizing ability and business capacity to become employers do not need financial assistance from the Government to provide the ordinary comforts of life or to make provision for old age. In every country, however, these constitute but a fraction of the total population; the majority will always be in the ranks of the artisans, labourers, and clerks. It is the welfare, of this large class of citizens on whose behalf I am trying to say a word to-day. They are not paupers, they are not looking for charity; but in my judgment they have a right to expect from the Government such reasonable asistance as will enable them to properly organize their homes and so secure for their children places to which they can look back in later years with happy recollections.
There are many thousands of industrious citizens in this country who have not been able to acquire owership of even the most modest house and lot. They have striven to educate their children and to maintain their families in a state of decent comfort, and this has absorbed their entire earnings and deprived them of the opportunity of saving enough to purchase homes. On the other hand, Sir, it is true that there are many thousands who, by sacrifices, known only to themselves, have secured a start in this direction and by slow degrees have extin-

guished the mortgages they had to assume and carry over a period of years. This class of people are the very salt of the earth. They have uncomplainingly and, as a rule, cheerfully, submitted to domestic economies that no man or family makes from choice; they have submitted to those economies with their eyes on the future.
With every year that passes it becomes more difficult for a man to make such a start. In most of our cities and towns the price of house property has advanced to such a point that the initial payment necessarily demanded by builders is beyond the capacity of the average workman. Consequently the difficulties have increased -so enormously that the need of
4	p.m. assistance is greater now than at any time in the past. Moreover, the cessation of building operations during the war has left this country with a shortage of homes, estimated by officials of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada at between 45,000 and 50,000 houses. The result is that two or three families are compelled to live in one house which was designed to accommodate one small family.
It must be apparent to hon. members that heroic measures are justified to relieve such a situation. It is that kind of thing, Sir, that leads to dissatisfaction, intensifies unrest, and awakens in the individual a sense of injustice, making him an easy prey for radical and revolutionary agitators. An industrious man with a family crowded into inadequate space becomes a disheartened and careless citizen. Every man needs some incentive to inspire him to make the best of his opportunities and to properly develop his talents, but such personal development is impossible without wholesome and happy home surroundings, and unfortunately these cannot be obtained by many thousands of artisans in the towns and cities of this country. Let such conditions prevail over an extended period, and we will establish here some of the most deplorable features characteristic- of urban life in Europe. Those are the conditions that breed communism and anarchism; whereas the individual home where one family can live in privacy with a reasonable degree of comfort inevitably produces a better type of parent and a better type of child. So I take the ground, Sir, that all governments should be concerned with the material and moral welfare of those they govern.
The problem of housing has become so acute that the need for extraordinary measures must be apparent to every
observant person. As I have already stated, officials of the Trade and Labour Congress of Canada have declared that there is a shortage of 45,000 houses. We find that the situation has become a matter of deep concern to the provincial legislatures, for I see by the press that legislation to place restrictions upon landlords has been suggested in the Legislature of Quebec, while in the province of Ontario the exorbitant rents charged by landlords, due entirely to the shortage of houses, has led the Government of that province to introduce a bill to establish a fair-rent court. This surely is an extraordinary measure and one which a few years ago no one would have dreamt of suggesting.
Addressing the Town Planning Convention at Toronto on February 17 last, Archbishop McNeil, said;
There are few of the six-roomed houses in Toronto that have not got two families in them, and sometimes lodgers besides.
Last year we had 7,784 marriages in Toronto, and at least 5,000 houses at reasonably low prices were called for. How many such houses were erected? Only 61. And we find that 116 houses were pulled down during the year, while 79 dwellings were converted into business places. So, you see, we have been progressing backwards.
I think I need go no further in elaboration of my argument of the necessity for a vigorous programme of house building in our towns and cities. The condition is so obtrusive that it is scarcely possible for any person to be ignorant of it.
It will no doubt be argued that the responsibility for improving housing conditions rests with the provincial governments. I admit the force of this argument, but it seems to me that this Parliament, being the chief legislative authority in the Dominion, might well undertake, in co-operation with the provincial and municipal authorities, a programme that would relieve conditions which are so unsatisfactory and which must tend towards the degeneration of our people. I appreciate what this Parliament has done in appropriating $25,000,000, of which $10,000,000 has been expended through the provincial authorites. However, that does not seem to me to go far enough. While the British North America Act may impose upon the provinces the responsibility of settling social questions of this kind, I do not think that that entirely absolves this Parliament of responsibility to take cognizance of, and to provide remedies for, conditions of so unsatisfactory a nature.
The germ of my proposal in this resolution is not to provide any temporary expedient, but rather to create a permanent

body that would constantly be available to prevent the intensification of this problem and to work in the direction of assuring to every man an opportunity to acquire his own home, providing he will make any real effort himself. This is not socialism, Mr. Speaker, it is individualism. It is not giving our people something for nothing. It is putting them in a position where they would be encouraged to exercise thrift, to develop industrious habits and thus steadily to liquidate the indebtedness that they must incur to become their own landlords.
The possession of real estate, no matter how small a portion, has a peculiar effect upon a man, and it is an effect that is shared by his family. It raises his standing in the community. It gives him a sense of dignity. That is one of the strongest incentives to self-development that any person can have. He becomes deeply interested in the good government of his municipality because he is a direct taxpayer, and this interest in municipal affairs inevitably leads to closer study of all other branches of government that we have. He follows the course of political discussions. He applies more intelligent methods in reaching dis decisions as to his political future. He feels himself to be an important unit in the body politic. Who can estimate the value to the country of converting the easygoing, rent-paying artisan into an earnest, property-owning citizen? The effort to acquire a home in this way arouses in the average man an ambition to develop every talent that he possesses. We have all through this country manufacturers and employers of labour who owe their present position in business to the thrifty habits acquired by the purchase of a home in their early years. It develops all that is best in a man, because he is not actuated by purely selfish motives; the welfare of his wife and family is the dominant idea in his mind. Thus the finer impulses of his nature are stimulated; he takes a pride in his little property because it is his, no matter how large the mortgage may be. A spirit of emulation causes him to employ his spare hours in making improvements and keeping his little property in the best condition he can. And, Sir, the effect upon his family is proportionate to that upon himself. His wife is as deeply interested in and is as proud of her ownership as her husband. Upon her falls a great deal of the necessity for thrift, and she benefits in every way by the responsibilities which she carries in common with her husband. The children in such a home are necessarily taught industrious and frugal habits, and

such teaching in childhood has its effect throughout life. The very obligations assumed by the parent are shared unconsciously by the children; at a tender age they learn to understand the value of economy, and ultimately see its reward in the liquidation of the indebtedness on their home and the better conditions under which they live. These things cannot be taught in school; it is only by the everyday experiences in the home that a child can be made to understand that self-denial in the small things is necessary for the accomplishment of a purpose which makes for the permanent welfare of the family. Such lessons as forming a part of the child's education should not be lightly regarded. So that for the man, for the woman, and for the child there is educational and moral value and the development of civic virtue in the ownership of a home.
Contrast the conditions outlined by Archbishop McNeil, where two or more families live in a six-roomed house, with the occupancy of a house by one family. A whole speech might be made on this phase of the housing problem. It is essential to the proper care and training of children that there should be privacy in the domestic circle. That makes for obedience to parental authority; it enables parents to bring up their children in their own way and without the dangers through associations beyond their control. The house with two or three families in it can never be dignified by the name of home. It may be a place in which to sleep, but all the wholesome influence of home that men cherish throughout their lives and which restrain them from excesses of all kinds are absent from those habitations where two or three families are herded together in six rooms. We make complaints about the inefficiency of the churches, and then we allow conditions to be created that render all the wishes of religious teachers to care for the spiritual welfare of the people difficult if not impossible of accomplishment.
In my judgment, Sir, the time has come when the state must do all that it reasonably can to restore the home to the place of power and influence which it ought to occupy and which in times past it did occupy; for to its occupancy of that place we are indebted to-day for the morality of our people and the stability of our institutions. We are now going through a crisis in this world as the aftermath of the great war, but it is a crisis that never would have arisen, I venture to say, if the common people of all the civilized nations had

been in possession of their own property. Ownership of real estate makes a man a steadier citizen. Having made the sacrifices inseparable from the acquisition of a home his whole interest lies in maintaining it. He is not fuel for agitators or revolutionists; on the contrary, he is an impediment to the agitator; he is the most desirable force in the country for orderly government and constitutional procedure. I take an ilustration from my own city, Sir, a community of half a million people. The extremes of wealth and poverty are to be found there, in a form quite as acute as in any city of the Dominion. Looking at it upon the surface, it would seem to be fertile ground for communist activity, but it passed safely through that period of unrest which affected similar communities in this country more seriously. What is the explanation, Mr. Speaker? It lies in the fact that forty-seven and one-half per cent of the houses in Toronto are occupied by their owners. Roughly speaking, one-half of our population have a deep sense of responsibility for good gevernment and the maintenance of order, to a degree that would not be possible if they had not been influenced by the possession of small properties which to them are as great as the plants of the wealthiest manufacturers. Is it not worth while, Mr. Speaker, for this Parliament to take cognizance of such a situation, and even to take extraordinary measures to bring about, by degrees, that state of affairs in which every man will have the same incentive to be an industrious and thrifty citizens? These periods of unrest will recur, we have not seen the last of them in Canada; and I submit that the best means that can be adopted to prepare to deal with such crisis is to develop to the highest degree that we can those qualities that make for sobriety of temperament, steady observance of the law, and intelligent co-operation for personal and community improvement.
We have been fortunate in this country in that we have so few large cities, and so many cities of from ten to thirty thousand population. I wish that the two or three large cities we have could be reduced one-half in population, and that the other half of their population could be spread throughout the smaller communities. I am sure that this would produce a much more wholesome state of affairs. My own province of Ontario is the best example that we have of the existence of few large cities. There are in that province scores of flourishing communities of a population
of from ten to thiry thousand, where workmen have their half-acre to cultivate and their own little cottage,where contentment and ideal domestic conditions prevail. There are cities like Kitchener, Guelph, Stratford, St. Thomas, and a score of others that ilustrate the point I am trying to make. In these places strikes are almost unknown, for employer and employee live together in harmonious relations, and in the last analysis, Mr. Speaker, It will be found that this state of industrial harmony can be traced to the ownership by the operatives in the factories of their own homes. They are better workmen because they are contented with the conditions under which they live, the most important factor of which is domestic felicity. They are good neighbors to one another because of the influence of happy homes. Let illness overtake one family in such a community as I am trying to describe, and from all sides will come assistance and sympathy and helpfulness, because they have been welded into one great family by long associations and intimate relationship.
Nor can we overlook the importance of a permanent abode in the life of a man and his family. Those who are at the mercy of landlords may live a year in one place and a year in another. Continual changes of residence are costly to the family; they lessen the ability of parents to own their own property, while they have a sad effect upon the children.
The ownership of a house and lot is insurance against unemployment and old age. In great Britain large sums of money are paid out in old age pensions and unemployment doles and there are advocates of like measures in this country. I do not entirely disagree with their view, but I look upon such payments as a form of charity that self-respecting men must accept with repugnance. It is better for the people, and for the State, to preserve the finer sensibilities of our citizens by putting them in a position to meet such emergencies by their own efforts. One who has not rent to pay monthly can get through a period of unemployment much more easily than one who must raise a definite amount for a landlord as the months roll by. The payment of rent has been the most difficult feature of the unemployment situation with which we have had to deal in our city during the last few months. The fear of eviction, added to the anxiety of enforced idleness, has intensified the distress of many a family. With that obligation eliminated, it is astonishing how

long a family can carry on with small means, and in most cases it is possible to get through several months of unemployment. Unemployment usually occurs in the fall and winter months when the need of shelter is imperative. As spring opens up in this country, work is resumed in many lines in which it is impossible during the rigorous winter season, so that if we could put the masses of our people in a position to tide over the few months of unemployment, which will always be an inevitable feature of Canadian life, we would accomplish a great deal for the wage earner.
Ownership of a home would also act as a provision for old age, and it would be more effective provision than the small dole which is the best any country can pay to the aged and infirm. Given a home in which to live, an ohl couple will require but little additional assistance to maintain them. That little, in nearly every instance, could be provided by the children who might share the home belonging to their aged parents. The amount which they would pay in rent would meet this obligation; or if the children have homes of their own, the rent their parents could receive from their own home

and there will always be a renting class-would be sufficient for the modest needs of the parents, so that the possession of house property, of a home, by a man and his wife, forms, to my mind, the most self-respecting provision that can be made for unemployment or old age.
An appropriation provided for this purpose would be, not an expenditure, but an investment, and one more certain of return than the vast sums which we are providing for the railways. The experience of loan companies in Ontario is that not one per cent of men who purchase homes on the instalment plan fail in meeting their obligations. Their first care is to meet the interest and principal payments, and they submit to economies of the most drastic kind when that is necessary to protect their little properties. Therefore, it must be conceded that there would be no losses to the treasury from such an undertaking.
I have proposed in the resolution that returned soldiers should have the preference in the expenditure of moneys appropriated for such a purpose. We owe that to them at least; we owe to the returned soldiers a great deal more than we ever can pay; many of them have come back and have not been able to settle down in homes and are still at the

mercy of landlords. The services that they rendered to us overseas require us to see that, whether they are living in the country or in the city, unusual measures are taken to bring about their re-establishment both in their occupation and in all the other phases of civil life. In fact, this is part of the re-establishment of the returned men. Those who live in the cities receive their gratuities, those who are able to go on to the farm receive a good deal more; and I think something more might be done than has been done in the way of re-establishment for soldiers having their domiciles in the cities or the country. This is one way that would prove effective and, I think, desirable, from their standpoint.
Perhaps the greatest criticism that can be brought against a proposal of this kind is: How would the fund be administered? The resolution suggests the creation of a Housing Board. My idea is that that should be composed of permanent officials, at least one of whom should be from the Department of Public Works, and that that Housing Board could, on behalf of the Government, enter into arrangements with loan companies now in existence and doing business in the Dominion of Canad-a. Those loans companies have had long and successful experience in conducting exactly this kind of transaction, and I have no doubt that arrangements could be made with such companies to take this money and lend it cut under their direction, control and responsibility. We would then have a responsible local body, assuring to the purchaser of a home that it would he properly built; that when a contract was let to a builder, there would be such inspection as would ensure that all the specifications would properly be carried out. The money would not be paid to the builder except in proportion as the work went on, and the great profits made by speculative builders would be eliminated. At the present time the speculative builder buys a lot; he puts up two or three houses; he puts what money he has into them; he borrows what the loan company will lend on them, and then when he sells them he takes second mortgages for all he can get. Under the plan I suggest, the prospective house owner would apply to the loan company; he would have the benefit of the advice of that company; and the profit of the speculative builder-and in many cases that is a considerable item-would

be saved to him. Another feature that is important in a plan of this kind is the collection of periodical instalments. If a Government board undertook to do that work, it would have grave difficulties, but that woi'k can be done through loan companies which would be financially interested, both in the building and in the collection of the accounts, and which would give the business the personal attention of a large and experienced staff. In that way the borrower would not be liable to the Government and could not come making a poor mouth; he would be liable to and would be required to deal with a business organization in a business way.
The reason why so many people desiring homes are unable to get them is that they must be prepared to pay down a sum equal to at least 40 per cent of the value of the property. Loan companies will lend about 60 per cent as a maximum. My proposition would be that a man should be able to get a home if he can pay down 10 per cent. If the Government were so deeply interested in the matter as to provide money, they could stand behind the loan company to the extent of 30 per cent. The man buying the house would be required to pay down at least $300 or $400-let us say $300, for the sake of illustration-on a $3,000 house. The Government would stand behind 30 per cent of the remainder, and the other 60 per cent the loan company would stand behind. It is certain that if we do not make it easier in the future than it has been in the past for men to own their own homes, the housing shortage will not only continue but will be aggravated, and conditions that are so bad now will become very much worse with almost every year that passes.

speechtext:
Did my hon.
friend ever know a person who got out of the hands of a loan company after getting into them?

subtopic: THE HOUSING PROBLEM. PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF A FEDERAL HOUSING BOARD
speechtext:
I have known a great
many people who have got into the hands of a loan company and got out satisfactorily. I got out myself once; that is the best answer I can give my hon. friend. I thought I had cleared up that point when I said that not one per cent of the people who buy houses from loan companies fail in meeting their obligations. That looks as though they got out and got out quite satisfactorily.
Under this plan it would be possible for groups of workmen to get together who have not the capital to form companies
of their own, and then take from the loan companies contracts to build these houses. I think if that were done you would get more efficiency from the builders than you have been getting in the past. During the past year brick layers were laying 700 to 800 bricks a day, and in some cases down to as low as 500. But if two or three bricklayers had a contract to put up a brick house they would lay from 1,500 to 1.800 bricks a day. As a matter of fact, on the new King Edward Hotel being built in the city of Toronto they laid 1,400 bricks a day this winter, while last summer they were laying only 600 to 700. I think if you got a group of carpenters, bricklayers and painters to co-operate, drawing their money as the work went on just as they would their wages, you would get a standard of efficiency in house building that has not been possible in the past and is not possible under any other conditions.
My idea is that the Housing Board would prepare a certain number of plans of six-roomed houses, and perhaps five-roomed, and even up to eight-roomed houses. These plans could be accepted and materials standardized. I think in the standardization of materials for the construction of such houses, and perhaps the purchase on the credit of the Housing Board of large quantities of such materials, enormous savings could be made. Each man building a house would be able to get his materials, or the greater part of them, through this Housing Board and would thereby effect a . very substantial saving- and economy is an essential feature of a programme like this.
I have not attempted to work out all the details, Mr. Speaker, because that can only be done from experience. I do not think any man could to-day lay down a plan that would not require considerable adjustment in future, but experience will enable us to make those adjustments. The point I want to lay before the House is that we are faced with a tremendous need in this country, and it is a need which if not filled will make for more difficult, and perhaps disastrous, conditions in the country. On the other hand, if the need is met and filled, we shall have entirely the opposite condition. Shall we attempt to solye this matter as a great social problem, or shall we say it is beyond our power? To say the latter would be, to my mind, the counsel of timidity. There are obstacles, of course, in the way of carrying out such a proposition, but we are here to overcome such obstacles. We are elected to look after thr welfare of the people of this country* ar.d

if we are incompetent to overcome these obstacles, that should only be decided after we have made an earnest attempt to find a>
solution. What is needed, Sir, is vision and courage. I believe that the bonds for such a purpose as I suggest would be taken up by our own people, and the money to meet the interest would be provided year after year as the work went on. I know there is a disposition not to increase the debt of this country, but this is not a debt, it is an investment. It is a form of social legislation that is already being practiced in some places where conditions have been allowed to grow up that made legislation absolutely imperative. The British government has carried out large housing schemes. Why? Because they had to, because conditions got so bad there was nothing else for them to do. If they had started fifty or a hundred years before living conditions in Great Britain would be very much better than they are to-day; and if we go on another forty or fifty years as we are doing, and the Government does not take any cognizance of the difficulties of the average workman and artisan of the country, conditions will grow up in our great cities similar to those in the great cities of other countries. To my mind that would be deplorable.
I do not think the need can be met by private capital. I think that has been demonstrated by our experience of the last year or two. To get a real solution there must be governmental assistance. So, in view of the urgency of the need, and of the enormous benefit that would accrue from the successful carrying out of the idea, I believe this is a matter that should enlist the sympathetic consideration of the Government, and one that warrants unusual methods on the part of this Parliament.

subtopic: THE HOUSING PROBLEM. PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF A FEDERAL HOUSING BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I agree with my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) in his remarks on the benefit to citizenship that comes from men owning their own homes. No better illustration of that could be given than conditions in the smaller cities and towns throughout the country, to which he pointed, where nearly all the working men own their property. That is the ideal situation for the community, because it makes these people take an interest in all that goes on in the community, and at the same time take an interest in their country. These men are very intelligent voters. There are seldom any strikes or troubles between labour and capital in the smaller cities and towns of this country. These men, however, in the

past have been able, without any assistance from the Government, to acquire their property, and in a great many instances have been able to pay for it, either through private loans or through loan companies or corporations of that kind. No matter how they acquired their property, they have acquired it. They have saved, and in so doing have shown their character. They have been able to buy their own properties and in a great many cases they live just as comfortably as anybody else in the land. I perfectly agree with all my hon. friend has said along that line. It would be a very desirable thing if we could get everybody in this country to own their own homes, and to take an interest not only in their local community but in the country at large. But he proposes that the Dominion Government should go into the loaning business. Now, I da not agree with my hon. friend when he says that where three families live in a six-roomed house, that is perhaps a good place in which even to sleep. I think the opposite. I do agree, however, with his statement that the possession of real estate has considerable effect on a man. I have experienced the truth of that several times, but the effect is perhaps not the same as that implied by my hon. friend. The effect has been a very undesirable one [DOT] sometimes, so far as I am concerned.

speechtext: You had too much of it.

subtopic: THE HOUSING PROBLEM. PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF A FEDERAL HOUSING BOARD
speechtext:
I had too much of the
kind. This question Mr. Speaker, came up before the Re-establishment Committee in the fall of 1919, and I think it is one that should go to the Re-establishment Board which is operating now. It came up before them and they submitted it to the Re-establishment Committee of this House, who considered it very carefully and reported against it because they thought that it was too dangerous an experiment for the Dominion Government to undertake. I should like to see every man own his own property, as my hon. friend suggests. He pictures the very happy condition that would exist if that were the case, and I agree absolutely with all that. But as to the Dominion Government undertaking to go into the loaning business, my hon. friend knows, as does everyone in this House, that there seems to be a peculiar feeling throughout the country that when any moneys can be got from the Government it does not matter very much whether they are repaid or not. For that reason I cannot share his confidence that the Government would not lose money by the proposal he makes. A few years ago, if I mistake not, we

passed a Bill in this House, authorizing the loan of $25,000,000, guaranteed by the provinces. I understand that most of the provinces have not availed themselves of that offer, although Ontario has to a certain extent; and I know that in some places in that province the scheme will entail a great deal of loss, because they are building houses which they cannot sell for anything like what it cost to put them up. I know whereof I speak, at least in one instance. In my judgment, while the hon. member who introduced the resolution is perfectly right in all he set forth this afternoon as to the desirability of people owning their own property, and on that account taking an interest in the country, and so forth, if there is any one outside of the corporations or private individuals who is going to lend money it ought to be the municipality. The municipalities have the means of knowing exactly the character of the borrower, and in the loaning of money, years of experience have taught me that a great deal more depends upon the character of the indivadual who borrows money then frequently upon the nature of the security itself. You can safely loan money to certain people with very little security, while you cannot loan it to others who offer what would apparently be good security, because, as we all know, securities depreciate very much sometimes. I have known them to go down fifty per cent in the course of ten years. And especially do securities in housing depreciate very materially through lack of care taken of the property. Some people take such excellent care of their property that after they have occupied it ten or fifteen, or even twenty years, it is in as good condition as it was when built, if not better. On the other hand, occupied by some other people, it would not, after such a period, be worth twenty-five per cent of what it originally cost. Let me repeat, that if there is any one going into the loaning business it should be the municipalities, for, as I say, they are able to obtain accurate knowledge as to the character of the borrower, and can judge accordingly. The municipality can lend money just as well as the Dominion Government, and they would know, by the character of the borrower, exactly whether they were running any risk in making a loan. My hon. friend suggests another commission. In my opinion, we have quite enough commissions already. I am opposed to another commission.

speechtext: Call it something else.

speechtext: A rose by any other name-you know the rest. After all, it would be a commission, and it would have to be paid for the work it undertook. They would have to be paid by the Government, or else take their expenses and their salaries out of the people to whom the loans were made, and that would not be beneficial to the borrower. Now, I am not going to take up much more time. I must, however, reiterate that I am absolutely opposed to the Dominion Government going into the loaning business.

I would commend to the mover of the resolution the suggestion I offer, that the municipality should take hold of the question, if it is a pressing one, in the city of Toronto. I know that the municipality from which I come will not ask the Dominion Government to loan them money. If they think that loans should be made they will look after this themselves.
Mr. W. If. BALDWIN (Stanstead): It is not often that I agree with the mover of the resolution, but in one respect he is right- in the principle that people should own their own property. Times have changed wonderfully in my day. Forty years ago practically every one was trying to get a piece of land on which to build a home, but since that time there has been a continual exodus to the cities and now there is more land for sale and there are more deserted homes in the country than there were, say, twenty years since. People seem to want to shirk responsibility. Very many young people will spend exorbitant sums in immoderate wedding presents, and often there is more money involved in the outlay of a wedding than would buy a small farm. People do not want to shoulder the cares and responsibilities of rural life and are therefore flocking in large numbers to the cities, where there seems to be the greatest frivolity. One has only to look at the picture shows, the candy shops, and other attractions, to see the inducement that is held out for country people to come to the city. I think that the Government, instead of helping people to own their own homes in the cities, should do something to retain the rural population on our farms. Any assistance given by the Government in the way of helping people to build homes, should be

given with the distinct understanding that the occupants will be kept busy producing something or other. Everything can be said for the person who owns his own house on a plot of land, however small, from which he derives an honourable livelihood. In my opinion, the Government will have to put a tax on a good many things if they want to keep people from leaving the country and coming into already overcrowded cities. What is needed more than anything else in my section of the country just now is good roads. I made an offer, through the public press, of from $20,000 to $40,000 to the township I live in towards the construction of stone and gravel roads. I could not get them to accept my offer even though I proposed to in that way bear one-third of the cost of the entire work that needs to be done.
Now, with respect to what the Qovern-ment has done in the way of helping the returned soldier let me say that from my observation a great many soldiers who have gone upon the land have made a success of it, but still a large number of the farms that were taken up for this purpose havp been thrown back again on the hands of the Government. And I believe it can be taken for granted that in the first place the Government paid for these farms far more than they were worth; in other words many of these farms could have been bought for fifty per cent less than was paid for them had the purchase been conducted in a businesslike manner.
The principle of the resolution is in the right direction but how are you going to carry it out? If you go into the rural sections of the country you will find in every township vacant houses. Surely it is not proposed to build more houses in the cities in view of the fact that the urban centres are already full of people that cannot get work. I read a short time ago that in the Niagara district they were running the great industries there at only twenty-five to thirty per cent of their capacity. While there are vacant houses in the country districts some steps should be taken to induce people to live in those houses and cultivate the soil. While the idea of everybody in the country owning their own house is a good one, and while there is not the least doubt that in the people who own their own dwellings you have the finest force of constabulary that you can possibly have, I do not think it would be wise to embark upon such a large expenditure of public money as the resolution contemplates.

Mr. WILLIAM GARLAND McQUAR-RIE (New Westminster): I should have been much better pleased if the mover of this resolution had asked for a further grant under the scheme which the Federal Government adopted in 1918, whereby it advanced money to the provincial governments, and the provincial governments in turn advanced money to the municipalities for the purpose of making loans to soldiers to enable them to build their own homes. So far as my experience has gone that plan worked out very well indeed, and I think the dwellings which were built were very much needed. In my opinion the building of those houses was a very good thing for the returned soldier. The object of that scheme has not yet been fully attained. The conditions still exist which would warrant the building of more houses for returned soldiers, and I think we might very well now ask that further grants be made under similar conditions. Before I left home I was handed a memorandum by the Great War Veterans' Association of New Westminster. The memorandum sets out certain arguments in favour of a further grant which I think are perfectly sound. These arguments are as follows:
1.	The object of the first appropriation has not been attained, viz; the alleviation of the shortage in housing accommodation. Rents are as high or even higher than in 1918 and the same shortage of houses exists.
2.	It is universally admitted that a community of people owning their own homes is a much greater asset to the state than a community of reni -payers. The ownership of a home creates a spirit of civic pride and fosters an interest in public affairs and community welfare which acts as a sedative to the present unrest and discourages the irresponsible agitator.
3.	To the returned soldiers, many of whom have only since returning from overseas assumed the position of head of a family, the scheme is of paramount benefit. The settling of these men in their own homes, where their tenancy is secure and they are not subject to exorbitant rents, and which puts within their reach a substantial dwelling which they would probably be unable to ocquire otherwise, is one of the most effective means of turning a soldier into a fully re-established citizen.
4.	The continuation of building operations at the present time would tend to relieve the present unemployment situation.
5.	The inauguration of a building programme at this time would necessitate large purchases of lumber and other supplies. This would have a stablilizing effect on the lumber market and would benefit the lumber mills which are now preparing to resume operations after a period of depression and uncertainty in the lumber trade. The purchase of other supplies from dealers in different trades would also tena to keep money in circulation and prevent stagnation in business during a trying time.
Now the member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) has said that if any one is going

to loan money for the purchasing or building of houses it should be the municipalities. Well, that is exactly what this scheme contemplates. The Dominion Government, as a matter of fact, only finances the provinces and they in turn finance the municipalities, so that the municipalities are really the ones who assume the responsibility for the indebtedness. The Dominion Government has a perfectly good security when it has the bond of the provincial governments, and the latter have a perfectly good security when they have the backing of the municipalities. My hon. friend from North Oxford also said that the municipalities could borrow the money just as well as the Government could. In that view I am afraid he was mistaken. My hon. friend, of course, has a good deal of knowledge in respect to financial matters, but I am inclined to think he made that statement without giving the matter much thought; it is well known that a municipality cannot borrow money on such good terms as a government can do; and the security of the Dominion Government is much better in the markets of the world than that of any municipality. The hon. member for North Oxford said furthermore that in his town they would not think of asking for any loan of this kind. That fact does not need to affect the situation in any way. My hon. friend's town does not necessarily have to take advantage of this plan, neither does any municipality which does not deem it advisable to go into the loaning of monies under this scheme. The municipality has to decide on the applications which are made, and if it considers it is not advisable to proceed with the scheme there is no obligation on its part to do so. It seems to me that the plan to which I have referred is a good one and should be continued. I know there are a large number of soldiers who find themselves more or less homeless and who would gladly take advantage of the opportunity of borrowing more money under the scheme which has been in force. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I would urge upon the Government the continuation of the former scheme of lending money for the purpose of helping our returned men to build homes.

The "fault" of the other

At the present time the business of this Government is not socialism, its business is to take care of the wants of all the people. This country offers sufficient opportunities to men of enterprise and energy to make their own way without being spoon-fed by the Government; perhaps there is no country in the world that offers such ample opportunities to every-



one. And yet we are called upon from day to day to pass special legislation taxing one citizen to enable other citizens to live in comfort and, in many cases, in idleness. Let each individual stand on his own feet. Let the Government legislate for all the people instead of giving special privileges to particular classes, and let the Government not interfere with trade unless that trade interferes with the rights of any of our citizens. Then we will have a country that will attract the best class of immigrants, because they will recognize that their success depends on their own initiative and resolution. Let us give all our people an equal standing. No man wants anything more; no man is entitled to anything more.
