Mr. Speaker, I did not expect to say anything on this resolution, not knowing that it would come Up to-day, but I was a little taken aback by the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) indulging in his usual hard knocks at the province of Ontario. Now, I did not think that this resolution had any-think in particular to do with the province of Ontario, but that it related to the whole Dominion. Although this resolution comes from a gentleman of very great ability, still, I consider it a very dangerous proposal, for several reasons. It would mean that the cities would take advantage of the proposed appropriation, as the country places would have no occasion to avail themselves of it- but of course they would have to do their share toward finding the money. Further, if this resolution became law we would have to organize a new department at great expense, and by the time we had paid the salaries of an architect and other officials
I MV. Cahill.]
to carry out the regulations a large sum of money would be spent apart altogether from that devoted to encouraging the building of homes. No doubt as long as the Government would do the building there would be any number of people ready to take the houses; and there is no question that there would be a very small return on the money loaned. But, apart from the heavy expenditure this proposal would entail, it would have the further disadvantage of taking away from our young men any incentive to exert themselves to provide their own homes-and we all know that in times past we had to work very hard to become our own landlords. And where is this going to end? We have old age pensions, we have soldiers' pensions, pensions for unemployment are going to be proposed, and I do not know what other suggestions of a similar kind. Any legislation to help our soldiers I am heartily in accord with, but legislation such as this resolution suggests would not enure to the general advantage of the country, and the Treasury cannot afford it. Our national debt stands at the stupendous figure of over $2,000,000,000, and with our other financial commitments I think we ought to be very slow to build houses for those who do not intend to work for themselves. But I think if one stipulation had been inserted in this resolution it would be very beneficial to our young men, namely, that the picture shows and theatres be closed so that what those young men earn during the day they may not spend at night. Then they might be able to save some money to build homes of their own. I think we would do well to restore to as great an extent as possible that free and independent spirit that prevailed in Canada among the early settlers in connection with their getting themselves established and building up homes in a new country for themselves and their families. I am against the resolution for the reasons which I have stated, although I support the idea that we should do all we possibly can for those deserving people who are in poor circumstances and cannot own their own homes. But as for encouraging the younger man or any man to waste his time or to indulge in habits of idleness in making him the offer of a house under the terms suggested, I will vote against it every time.

subtopic: THE HOUSING PROBLEM. PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF A FEDERAL HOUSING BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I agree with the general remarks of the mover (Mr. Hocken) of the resolution. I believe, as I think we all do, that the home is the foundation of character

and the foundation of our country, and coming as I do from a city the major1 ty of whose inhabitants own their own homes, I know the value to a community of a home-owning population. If, therefore, I attempt to criticize some features of the suggestions made, I do not do so from any desire of decrying the main idea.
In the first place, it has been suggested, not by the mover but by a subsequent speaker, that the Government might enter the lending business. That, I think, would be q grave mistake. In 1914, and early in 1915, the Government saw fit, under extraordinary circumstances, to make large grants to certain of the farmers in the West-grants which in the majority of cases resulted in a wonderful return both to the men themselves and to the country at large. I believe that-speaking from memory-out of about $12,000,000 advanced for seed grain, fodder and relief at that time, there is still owing on account of principal, not taking interest into consideration, something like $2,000,000. It is difficult to persuade borrowers from a government to repay, as they will and must repay a private corporation. I was much struck by a speech delivered in Moose Jaw not long ago by Mr. Dunning, the provincial treasurer of Saskatchewan, in which he was reviewing the operations of the Saskatchewan Farm Loan Board. He pointed out that in respect of loans made over a period of some three years-I do not think the board has been operating longer than three years-amounting to about $6,000,000, there were now $300,000 of interest in arrear. Mr. Dunning said in the frankest way, as is his wont: "When a man borrows from the government, about the last thing he seems to think it necessary to do is to repay, and I tell you gentlemen, unless our borrowers change their methods, our whole scheme will break down." However, the mover has suggested that instead of the Government entering the lending business, money should be advanced, as I understand it, by Government through loan corporations who would be entrusted with the lending of the money and with the perhaps more arduous task of collecting repayments. I do not know that that is impossible, but it could hardly be done free of charge. I have been able to go into calculations as to the cost only since the resolution was moved this afternoon, and I am afraid that difficulties might be produced which are not in the minds of hon. members. Take the case instanced by the mover, of an investment in a property of $3,000, ten per cent being provided by the 731
borrower and the balance, $2,700, being obtained by him through loan. I take it that the amount mentioned, $3,000, was supposed to be sufficient to pay for both lot and building, otherwise the loan would have to be larger or the borrower would, have to put up more money. Well, if we assume that the lot and the building would cost $3,000-and I am afraid that the cases in which both could be obtained for that amount are somewhat rare-we have first'to agree what rate of interest would be paid; nothing was said about that. I have to guess the rate; I place it at seven per cent,-that is distinctly below the present market rate in a good many of the provinces. The Government could hardly borrow to-day any considerable amount of money in Canada at less than six per cent. Then, the company charged with the supervision of lending and collecting would have to get about one per cent per annum, and even at that rate they would not be too well paid if the work were properly done. With interest at seven per cent; with taxes at an average rate of thirty mills; with an assessment at the rate of ninety per cent of the value of the propery; with insurance, and with a certain amount by way of repayment on principal, a payment of about $400 a year would be required from the borrower of $2,700, at least for the first few years,-his interest bill would, of course, decrease as his principal was reduced. Now, I leave it to the House whether the average borrower who put up ten per cent, or $300, at the outset, could fairly be counted upon to supply $400 per annum with which to carry on. Much would depend, of course, upon his occupation, his rate of wage, and his success in finding work throughout the year.
It is quite true, as was said by the mover, that the number of foreclosures or sales by loan companies, at least in Ontario, has been very small. That has been due, perhaps, to two causes. In the first place, prices, both of real estate and of building, have generally been rising, and if the original borrower were unable to pay he could always find some one to take over his bargain-some one, perhaps, in a better position to meet the debt and finally pay it off. In the second place, we must not lose sight of the fact that while, in the pre-war days, loan companies were prepared to lend up to, say, sixty per cent of the value of a house as established by an independent person, I doubt very much whether they would agree to-day to lend more than fifty per cent, having regard to present values and prices. Nor is it diffi-

cult to understand why, because in the February issue of the Labour Gazette, page 250, the index number on the first of January of this year relating to the wholesale prices of building materials-the prices of forty-eight different kinds of materials in various sections of the country being taken as a basis-was 347.1, as compared with 140.6 for January, 1913. In other words, building materials have increased in cost nearly two and one-half times in the last seven years. I happen to know that some companies, while they are prepared to lend half the value of real estate, limit their loans on buildings to 331 per cent of their present cost. If under the plan suggested we are to make a loan of 90 per cent of the present cost and to insist upon repayments of principal

and this is the only safe method of conducting such a business-we have an entirely different situation from that confronting loan companies lending 50 or even 60 per cent of the cost. I for one would fear that in many cases there would, of necessity, be default, and if the loan company were compelled, as I presume it would be, in carrying out its bargains with the Government, to take proceedings, too often the original builders or owners would lose such money as they had put into their homes. There is a vast difference between an owner who has an equity of 40 or 50 per cent in his home and one who has an equity of 10 per cent. Something was said, I suppose jocularly, to the effect that you never get out of a loan company's hands. The last thing, in the world a loan company wants is to get property on its hands; that is not its business. I can only speak for the mortgage company with which I am connected, and I can say that for thirteen or fourteen years at least, we have had no property on our hands. As a matter of fact, while twenty years ago, we were lending to farmers and others in the immediate vicinity of our offices millions of money, we are to-day borrowing from those same men an equal or greater amount which in turn we lend to others who are starting in life as they did. We are lending it out very largely to western farmers who, I have every belief and hope, will repeat the experience of their Ontario brothers and be, before long, in the market as lenders rather than as borrowers.
One w'ord as to the soldiers. We have, as has been said, considered this question more than once. To my mind, the great difficulty arose from this question:	If
we are to have a scheme for allowing a
[Mr. Cronyn. j
soldier to build a home, and if we are to advance to him 80 or 90 per cent of the cost thereof, what can we say to the soldier who has a mortgage already on his home? Must we not make an advance to him if we can get that money at a lower rate? What can we say to the man who wants to buy out a business? Must we not advance money to him to enable him to establish a business? Is not that essentially re-establishment? And are there not many other proposals equally deserving, equally of advantage to the country, to which we could hardly say "no," if we start in the business of advancing money to soldiers for any other purpose than that one now in force, namely, agricultural settlement?

subtopic: THE HOUSING PROBLEM. PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF A FEDERAL HOUSING BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think we are indebted to my hon. friend and colleague in the next constituency to mine (Mr. Hocken), for bringing this matter before the House, and I desire to say a word or two in support of his resolution. He has pictured in a very lucid manner, and apparently as a result of much thought, a condition of domestic life which is not attended by proper comfort and safeguards. His experience for many years as controller and mayor in a large city has enabled him to speak with authority on these matters. I have been told by others, and I know myself, that in large cities now the housing situation is becoming so acute that something must be done, because the congestion makes a squalor which is bound to have an evil effect upon families and, indeed, one might say that it affects the morality of the people. A condition where there are three or four families in a seven-roomed house with a community of kitchen arrangements, and that sort of thing, cannot but have an evil effect and get us into the same condition which has been fought now for fifty or sixty years in the slums of the large cities of Europe. England and Scotland have known that, despite all the arguments against such a proposition from an economic standpoint, it is not the theory of economics that must be considered, but the condition that exists that must be met. That shows the importance of dealing in a serious manner with the resolution which is now before the House.
It is quite true that many of the remarks which fell from the lips of the hon. membe* for Oxford North (Mr. Nesbitt) may be agreed with, and yet dissented from on the ground that this is a condition of affairs which is fast becoming desperate. The remarks of my hon. friend, whose advice on

these matters is always listened to with attention in this House, should not have too much effect upon hon. members, because of the very careful, cautious manner in which he deals with a business proposition. The result of his remarks was to throw a wet blanket, so to speak, upon an admirable proposition. You cannot look at these things solely from a business standpoint at the present time, because with the return of the men from the war and their inability to cope with conditions of life on account of either mental or physical derangement, such a situation has been produced that the country must step in and, to some extent, be paternal in its efforts. I think the lending of money in the Northwest for grain is a totally different category from the present idea. Lending on wheat is lending on personal property, making a personal loan, and if some of that-only $2,000,000 as it appears-has not been repaid, that is unfortunate, but it is due to the condition that it is personal property and you have only the personal promise of the individual. But erecting buildings by Government, financing and keeping as security the buildings which you erect, means a loan which must be listed, in a totally different category. There is the building and the lot which cannot be removed, and you have not merely the personal promise of the occupant, but the building and the land themselves. Therefore, the security is infinitely better, and I do not think the House should be influenced to frown upon a motion of this kind where the security always seems to be in hand and not dependent altogether on the personal character of the borrower. It is true a careful loan company will get reports on the personal character of those to whom it proposes to loan money, and if it finds that the applicant is reckless or a spendthrift it will not lend to him-but that is largely for their own convenience because they do not wish to have to take over land on which they have loaned money.
The great advantage in a scheme of this kind, of building many houses, is that the cost is made so much less because of the standardization of the different parts, and because of the wholesale purchase of materials. Bricks and lumber, for instance, could be got wholesale from the manufacturers instead of each man buying individually, and by standardizing window frames and other articles you would get a very much cheaper general cost.
My hon. friend from London (Mr. Cronyn) has put in a word of caution against going into a scheme of this sort
as an aid to returned soldiers, on the ground that it may be demanded that the scheme be extended to men who wish money to start up in business, to men who already have houses on which there is a mortgage and which they ask to be relieved from, or to men who wish to obtain their money at a cheaper rate. These difficulties no doubt exist, and the demands may be made, but if you have a clear-cut proposal in the first place for the building and financing of houses in order to alleviate the dreadful condition in some of our cities, I think we can look with equanimity on what is likely to happen in the way of demands from other sources. If it is not possible for us to go further than this particular scheme, let us say so, and not refuse to go in,to, a good scheme simply because other and further demands may be made.

speechtext:
My idea on that is very clear. This scheme cannot be put through except in a community or block, and every community should run its own business affairs. Overhead expenses and depreciation should be provided for jointly by the community and the householder. Of course, I speak now more with reference to the scheme referred to by my hon. friend from North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) with regard to block communities near large cities, meant chiefly for returned soldiers who are not able to obtain housing accommodation under present conditions. My hon. friend is mistaken if he thinks that matter is not before the Pensions and Re-establishment Committee this year as it was before. I have not pressed it very hard because I have had in mind that the people of this country have not yet appreciated what has been done in the Old Country and the United States along these lines. When we think of the immense increase in the value of property in the model villages in the Old Country,

owing to scientific management, architectural design, and beauty of landscape, we need not be alarmed at all as to any losses occurring. I am told that properties in Letchworth have increased by one-third in appraised value, just because of the popularity of the life which these model villages afford. This refers to a model village or block town near to a large centre. Undoubtedly, despite the protest of my hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Boyce), these are meant for the town man. We have already looked after the farmer, or those who can become farmers, by our Soldier Settlement plan. But there are other men who are in the most unfortunate position of having given up their little business or trade in the town when they went to the war, and who find when they come back that they are not able to make their way. Now those men should be looked after by the country just as much as, if not more than the men who can go on the farm and make a success of it. While the object of the motion is to provide these residences in towns, for city men, I do not think the people of this country will dissent from that at all, because they know of so many men who have been unable to make their way and provide proper housing for themselves and their families. The man from the city who comes back from the war and finds that he cannot get back the business he practically sacrificed is in a dire plight. He may by vocational training, perhaps, learn to make his living in some other way, yet he has not the money to house his family properly, and this is a scheme, not to give him the money, not to provide any dole or charity-because the instalments to be applied on purchase should be rigidly insisted on

but to assist him in getting a home for himself and his family. Of course, if you are going to play the game of giving in to every man who cannot pay his instalment, who makes a poor mouth and writes letters to the paper, and gets ill-advised people to fight for him, the scheme will fail. The commission must rigidly insist on the terms of purchase being complied with; And if that is done, the country will be at no loss. On the other hand, these little communities will increase in value and will greatly contribute to the happiness and content of a vast number of people, and will prevent many from slipping into slum life and becoming degraded both in morals and living conditions generally.

subtopic: THE HOUSING PROBLEM. PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF A FEDERAL HOUSING BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not able to agree with my two estimable friends from Toronto,

for, contrary to the expectation of my hon. friend from Pontiac (Mr. Cahill), I am not one of those who believe the government should go into a housing scheme on a wholesale scale. I have had a little experience in houses myself, and if the Government want to lose money I would recommend them to go into a housing scheme on a large scale. I do not think we are in a position to risk the finances of our country in such a scheme as my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) has laid before us. The reason houses are scarce today is because it does not pay to build them; that is the reason pure and simple. If you can make housing a profitable investment, capital will be found to build houses, but under the conditions which now obtain in the building trade it is not possible to buy land and build a house in any of our towns and cities and make 5 per cent clear. That has been my experience, and I think I am well within the mark. I believe one would make a good deal less than 5 per cent. After the local taxation is paid, and after insurance repairs, burst pipes, and all the rest of it, are attended to, owners of houses will find that their rental bill has dropped very materially, and I leave it to any hon. gentleman who has experience in the renting of houses-I am speaking of those that rent at a moderate rate-whether it is not a very poor-paying business, and one that brings endless trouble to owners. I want to point out that if the Government is going into the housing scheme, it is going to drive out individual effort along that line. That fact should not be forgotten, and that is precisely why fewer houses are being built to-day than should be the case. Private investors have become afraid that the Government is really going into building as a business. I have just made a rough calculation that there are probably 2,000,000 homes in Canada, that is, allowing about four and half to five persons per home-and I think that is a moderate estimate. Suppose twenty-five percent of these required government help to house them properly-that would be a fair proposition. That would leave 500,000 homes to be provided. Take these at the moderate price of $3,000 each and you have $1,500,000,000 invested in (homes for twenty-five per cent of the people, or a proposition about equal in magnitude to the nationalization of the railways of Canada. Now, if the Government is going to take the place of the private investor, it ought to take the whole field, because the private investor who has to pay 7 per cent for

his money cannot compete with the Government, or with government-aided houses that are paying 5 or 6 per cent. Private investors, under such circumstances, will not enter the field. I have seen some very good articles in British reviews lately on this question. Lady Selborne, I think, has written two or three articles, after very close consideration of the housing scheme, and she gives an analysis of the .question with which the British Government is faced, the situation there being very much more acute than in Canada; and she points out that if the Government implements the scheme it has under consideration, it will tax the national financial capacity to its utmost. Surely, in the present state of the finances of Canada, we do not want to embark on a scheme that will cost as much as I have stated, and not $50,000,000 as this resolution suggests. Why, $50,000,000 could be consumed in the city of Toronto alone.

subtopic: THE HOUSING PROBLEM. PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF A FEDERAL HOUSING BOARD
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: THE HOUSING PROBLEM. PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF A FEDERAL HOUSING BOARD
speechtext:
And in the city of Montreal there would have to be spent a considerably larger sum. Every town and city in Canada would also call for some expenditure, if the Government took hold of the proposition on a proper scale. In the finality, the scheme practically amounts to the nationalization of the homes in Canada, by which I mean those houses which people cannot afford to build for themselves.
Now, the returned soldier is in quite a different position. If he wants help, I say by all means let him have it, whether it is to build a home or to establish himself in business, or on a farm. For that I hold up both hands, if the country can afford it. But if any great industry-and I speak now as one who is somewhat interested in industry-finds its own men are not properly housed. I say that it is the duty of the manufacturer to put up houses, to see that his employees are housed as they should be. I stand for that; I believe it is a sound principle. I think that some manufacturers in Canada have done this, and all model factories that want to look after their hands properly know that one of the first considerations in the problem of maintaining stable help is to have employees well paid, and well housed, as far as possible, in fairly close proximity to the works. Of course, it is not possible to house them too close to the factories, but accomodation could be found for them away from the smoke and annoyance of their work and yet within easy walking distance. That is possible in all our smaller
towns and cities, although it is out of the question in Toronto, Montreal, and two or three of the larger centres. My contention, in brief, is, that the sum required for housing the people of Canada should not be spent for any one city, but for all our cities, and for the country as well if the people there require it. I say, house every one if you are going to enter into this business at all. If you are going to lend money to builders of all houses that are required, I believe my figures will be found to be fairly conservative, and I estimate that it will take about $1,500,000,000 for the initial expense of a housing scheme at present. Building material is at present out of sight, so to speak, and you will not get houses to-day for $6,000, which five or six years ago you could build for $3,000. The present, therefore, is not a good time at which to embark on the building business on a large scale, because the man who builds to-day on 5 per cent money may find that within two or three years his margin of 2 per cent on interest will have shrunk to such an extent by the falling market, which I expect in the near future in building materials, and possibly in labour, that this $6,000 house will have shrunk to $4,000. So that if he had a margin of safety of $2,000, that would be wiped out under existing conditions of building. If he built a $4,000 or $3,000 house he ought to have from $30 to $35 per month for it, and that is a large rent for a working man to pay. It is more than he should be called upon to pay, but it is not more than is demanded in all our towns to-day. People are asked to pay from $30 to $35 and even more per month. Therefore, with all deference to my hon. friend from West Toronto, I hope he will not try to induce the Government to embark on a scheme of such magnitude as this would undoubtedly be. It cannot be undertaken on a small scale if it is to be equitable, and as the scale it calls for is out of the question, I trust that the House will not sanction this proposal involving an expenditure of $50,000,000, because it would not settle the question. This sum is a mere bagatelle to what is required, and would not be of any benefit to those who borrow money and build today, because they would lose on their proposition by the shrinkage I have pointed out. And as the resolution stands, it calls for something which this Government has never been asked to do before. Let the cities, and the manufacturers particularly, look after the housing of their own people, and if the soldiers require homes, as I think they do, then that should be looked

after by the committee that has been appointed, and which will probably bring in a recommendation on the subject. I trust the motion will not be seriously considered by the House.
Mr. G. W. ANDREWS (Winnipeg Centre)-: I have listened with a great deal of interest to the many arguments in this debate, and I am still firmly of the same opinion as at the outset, namely, that there is a great shortage of houses in Canada. I am under the impression that if our health by-laws were properly enforced in Winnipeg, we should have somewhere in the neighbourhood of 20,000 people without homes at all. This is a state of affairs that has to be met some time, somehow, and if we are not competent to meet it, I have not the slightest doubt that some other bunch of legislators will come who will be able to deal with the matter. People have to live in decent houses, and, as I say, by some means or other, this problem must be faced. I was somewhat annoyed by a remark of one hon. gentleman who said that he was not in favour of this Government going into schemes of this kind, because he believed in people standing on their own feet. I feel compelled to point out to that hon. gentleman that there are many citizens of Canada who have not two feet to stand on; they lost them in the war. My particular object in rising now is to refer to that phase of the subject.
The hon. member who moved the resolution referred particularly to the returned soldiers. Now, we already have a Special Committee sitting which is empowered to investigate their affairs, and as it is very apparent to my mind,-as I am sure it will be the wish of hon. members-that if any class at all should receive consideration it should be this class, and bearing in mind the fact that they undoubtedly would be the first class to receive such consideration, I think the debate has reached the stage where we might well pass the subject on to the Soldiers' Committee. Under the circumstances, with the permission of the House, I would move the adjournment of the debate.

That, in the opinion of this House, it is in the interest of good government, that Ministers of the Crown should he permitted to sit in either Chamber, whenever measures and policies are introduced affecting their respective departments.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I regret that the Government benches are practically empty. In the good old days ministers were in their seats betimes, but after having passed through so many embarrassments of late perhaps the tardy attendance of the members of the present ministry is not to be wondered at. At all events, Mr. Speaker, I shall proceed with my resolution. I have brought it forward with a view to expediting the business of the House, believing it to be a reform well worthy of adoption by this Parliament.
At Confederation we adopted the bicameral system. I know there are some people in the country, and perhaps in this House, who think that we should be satisfied with one chamber; but I believe that there is a large body of public opinion which stands for an upper chamber. No doubt our upper chamber might with advantage be reformed in certain respects, but I am confident that I am in the right when I assert that the mass of the people are in favour of the continuance of the bi-cameral system.
Personally, I am in favour of an upper chamber.	First, because it was instituted for the protection of minorities in our Confederation. Second, because the representatives of certain of the provinces which united to form the Dominion feared that the predominance of the larger provinces in Parliament might perhaps prejudice the interests of the smaller ones, and they therefore insisted on the establishment of an upper chamber. Third, because I have an ingrained respect for the pact of Confederation itself. That pact is sacred to all the provinces, and their representatives should see that no encroachment is made on our constitution.. And then, as Sir John A. Macdonald said, when he pleaded in favour of an upper chamber at the time of the Confederation debates:
A second chamber has been recognized in all democratic countries as a check against ill-considered and hasty legislation.
If this was true under normal conditions, it is still more so to-day when the world is passing through a crisis and as an aftermath of this great war there is in all parts of the world an agitation for reconstruction. The term " reconstruction " may cover many iniquities, and in order that we in this country may have the advantage of

a real reconstruction-a reconstruction which will be in the best interests of the country and which will he carried out in a spirit of respect for the constitution and for the rights of all classes of the community-I believe that an upper chamber is perhaps even more necessary now than under normal conditions.
And Sir, much as the upper chamber might be criticized, I believe that on many occasions it has given evidence of real independence of thought and action. Not later than two years ago many senators, appointed by the present Government, were not afraid to cast their votes against what I believed was ill-considered and hasty legislation, a legislation which may perhaps very seriously involve the future of Canada itself. I refer to their vote on the very important issue of the acquisition of the Grand Trunk Railway system.
I do not say, Mr. Speaker, that there is no room for Senate reform. For instance, I believe that there should be an age limit, and perhaps a change in the mode of selection of the gentlemen who occupy seats in the upper chamber. I have always thought that the election of senators might in itself be a very good reform-election by legislatures, boards of trade, universities, and such public bodies. Of course, that is another question; I simply mention it this evening because I do not wish it to be thought that this resolution means something which it does not mean. Some of my friends on both sides of the House have thought that perhaps I was favouring the appointment of Cabinet ministers to the Senate. Mr. Speaker, we cannot afford to allow the upper chamber to be without representatives of the Government; we must face the situation that there will always be at least a leader representing the Government in that body, and occasions will arise when it will be necessary to have Cabinet ministers in the Senate. I do think, however, that mostly all Cabinet ministers should occupy seats in the popular chamber and that the less there are in the upper chamber the better for the Government and better for Canada. At all events, if any Cabinet ministers have to sit in the upper chamber, it is to be hoped that the Government, whether Liberal, Conservative or Agrarian, will always see to it that ministers in charge of spending departments sit in the popular chamber. I think that is a sound principle.
In England we have the time-honoured House of Lords; several ministers of the Crown sit in that chamber. I do not know
how many members of the present British Government sit in the House of Lords, but I know that certain of them do, and not the least important of them, at that. In England there have been cases where even the Prime Minister sat in the upper chamber; I recall the names of Lord Beacons-field, Lord Salisbury, Lord Rosebery. But in all those cases, which were exceptional cases, the Government was represented in the popular chamber by most brilliant and distinguished men who really carried public opinion with them,-Gladstone, Balfour, Asquith, Lloyd George; and I could name several others. But I believe that in England the day has gone by when prime prime ministers shall sit in the upper chamber. Thqugh tradition means much in that country, yet with the new wave of public opinion and with the reforms which have come gradually-indeed, the constitution itself is made up of precedents which come slowly down from year to year-I believe that the force of public opinion in England will not now stand for that practice and in days to come the prime minister, representing public opinion, representing the new democracy, will have a seat in the popular assembly and there propound the policies of the government. Of course, the government will always be represented by some very eminent minister in the upper chamber.
The Commons, Mr. Speaker, has been and is to-day the great inquest of the nation. To the Commons belongs the most important problems of government. To the Commons must be announced the policies of the government. Indeed, the House of Commons is the great lever of the British constitution. True it is that no Bill, no Act of Parliament, is perfect or complete without the sanction of His Majesty the King; all measures are sanctioned by His Majesty the King, the House of Lords and the House of Commons. But everybody feels that the great driving power in matter of legislation belongs to the House of Commons, and it is right that it should be so.
Now, Mr. Speaker, though I am a traditionalist-and I am not ashamed to say that I am a traditionalist-the realities of life will perforce bring some radical changes. Of course, as I have intimated, as 'long as we have the bicameral system- and I hope we shall maintain it-the government of the day must be represented in some way in the Senate.

But I do not see why a minister sitting in the upper chamber or in the House of Commons should be debarred from appearing in the other chamber, without having a right to vote. I do not see why a minister of the Crown sitting, for instance, in the upper chamber, should not have a right to appear before the House of Commons to explain the policies of his department and to answer questions when the Estimates of his department arp scrutinized in the House. Nor do I see why the gentlemen who occupy the Government benches in this House should not be allowed to appear in the upper chamber to give there such explanations as may be required of them. There is nothing new under the sun. This system which I am now propounding is the system followed in France, where it is not necessary that a minister of the Republic should even be elected by the people, and I suppose that would suit many of my hon. friends who have, at the present njoment, cabinet aspirations. This happens very often. But presently, M. Briand is a member of the Chambre des Deputes. The old tiger, M. Clemenceau, was also a member of one of the two Houses, I forget whether it was the Senate or the Chambre des Deputes. M. Leygues, who was defeated a few weeks ago, is a member of the Chambre des Deputes. The ministers at all events are not necessarily members of the French Parliament, and ministers in France can be summoned to appear on different occasions before either the popular assembly or the Senate. Last year I was a very close follower of the sessions of the French Parliament, and I could see one afternoon, for instance, a minister of the Republic appearing before the popular assembly, giving explanations, answering questions and passing from that assembly to the Senate sitting at the Luxembourg Palace. It is simply common sense that ministers of the Crown in Canada should have the same privilege. Both Houses should have the same right, because I claim as a right, on the part of any member, that when a policy is presented to the House, if the minister who has prepared, laid out, planned and initiated that policy, sits in the other chamber, he should be amenable here to explain that policy, to answer questions, to accept amendments. When the budget of such a minister's department is being debated before this House-and this is the only branch of Parliament which can discuss and debate at length the budget of a department and move for its 
reduction at the request of a member. I think it is simply commons sense that members of this House should have the right to summons the minister whose policy is questioned or whose budget is criticized. I stated a moment ago that in such an occurrence I would not give to the minister, belonging to the other chamber and appearing before this House, a vote; but he would speak freely in the House; he would explain as many times as necessary, and he would, therefore, help in framing the legislation and in directing the policy of the Government which, in the final result, becomes the policy of Parliament.

speechtext: Would the hon. member allow a minister sitting in a chamber other than the one to which he belongs, to make a motion?

subtopic: THE HOUSING PROBLEM. PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF A FEDERAL HOUSING BOARD
speechtext:
That, of course, is a question of detail which might be framed in the amendment which would be necessary to the rules of the House; but at first sight, I would say: No. I would say that he could suggest to one of his colleagues, or to any other member of the House, the main features of the motion, and he would be allowed to speak in support of it. I would not give him more power than he is entitled to. We, the members of the popular branch of Parliament, are vested with special powers; our rights, so to speak, are sacred. We hold those right directly from the people; we have a right to discuss; we have a right to condemn; we have a right to amend; we have a right to denounce, under certain rules. My object, it seems to me, is a common sense one. I will give some concrete examples of what trouble can be caused by the absence from this House of ministers who have seats in another chamber. My object is to bring ministers sitting, let us say, in the Senate, before the House of Commons, to explain their policies, to defend their Estimates and to accept whatever amendments are suggested by the House. At the present time, three ministers of the Crown have seats in the upper chamber, the Minister of the Interior, the Minister of Labour and the Postmaster General. The Minister of Labour is, it seems to me, essentially a representative of the people. I perhaps can understand why the present incumbent is in the upper chamber. I certainly will not minimize the ability and, I believe, the honesty of purpose of the present Minister of Labour I had some dealings with the hon. gentleman whep he was president of the Telegraphers' Union, and I was Minister of

Labour in a former administration, and I wish to say openly and publicly that my official relations with him at that time were certainly of the best, and undoubtedly in the interests of labour. I am sure you will appreciate, Mr. Speaker, that the place of the Minister of Labour is essentially in the House of Commons. He represents the labouring masses of this country, among whom we know there is at present quite a feeling of unrest. We may be called upon at any moment to pass legislation directly affecting the labouring masses. In fact, the most important legislation to come before us, the tariff legislation, affects labour to a very considerable degree. It therefore seems to me that the Minister of Labour ought surely to be in the House of Commons, but the Government, in the exercise of their right, have chosen to appoint him with a seat in the upper chamber.
Leaving aside for the moment the publication of labour statistics and the Labour Gazette, let us consider only one phase of his work, the administration of the Industrial Disputes' Act. The wise administration of that Act, affecting as it does, all public utilities in Canada, is certainly of the utmost importance to the country. Last year, my right hon. friend the leader of the Government (Mr. Meighen) was in charge of a Bill initiated by the Labour Department, amendments were sought affecting the Industrial Disputes Act, and my right hon. friend with all his ability, with all his astuteness, had to report progress on two or three different occasions because he was not sufficiently informed on the matter. Now if there is a man in the House whose legal acumen* is admitted by all, it is certainly the leader of the Government, but on that piece of legislation I well remember that he was obliged to report progress in the dying days of the session in order to confer with his colleague the Minister of Labour. There was a case which I think shows the necessity of an amendment to our rules so that; the minister would be in a position when legislation affecting his department was before the House to come and explain his policies to the House.
Take the case of the Minister of the Interior. If I mistake not, there has been grafted upon the Department of the Interior the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment. Now, every member of this House, and nearly every family in the ridings which we represent, is deeply interested in the civil re-establishment of our soldiers. Then as to the Department of the
Interior itself, it is a vast department affecting the whole of the Northwest Territories, with its wonderful, potential natural resources. It would not be too much to say that the future of Canada lies, in great measure, in the wise and safe administration of that department. My right hon. friend the leader of the Government, who presided over the Department of the Interior for a few years, knows that it is certainly one of the most important departments of the Government. Well, it so happens this year that the minister in charge of that department is the leader of the Government in the Senate Chamber. Is it fair, Mr. Speaker, that this House should be deprived of the ability of that hon. gentleman, for he is certainly one of the ablest men I have met, and of the benefit of his explanations when matters affecting his department are under discussion? Is it fair that he in turn should be deprived of the benefit of the constructive criticism that we sometimes have to offer to the very involved legislation that from time to time is initiated in connection with his department? I think every one will admit that if the Minister of the Interior had a seat in this House instead of in the upper chamber, it would be far better for the country. But it so happens that he sits there and I again put the question I put a moment ago:	Does not common sense dictate
that we so amend our rules as to bring that minister into this House whenever legislation affecting his department is under consideration here?
I now come to the Post Office Department. Here is a large spending department, which affects every constituency, every city, every town, every village, from the Atlantic to the Pacific ocean. The Postmaster General not only looks after the administration of his department here in Ottawa, but from my own experience I know that the reports from the various inspectors come directly to him and that no post office is opened in even the smallest village in Canada without the matter first coming under his survey. One can see by the questions that are put on the Order Paper, and by the motions for the return of papers, how the administration of that department concerns every member of the House of Commons. The Postmaster General sits in the upper chamber; and I know that for many years, because of the absence of that minister in another House, we have not been able to have even a proper debate on the huge expenditures of the Post Office Department.

This is not satisfactory; it is not fair; it is not just. And if the Government will persist in keeping the Postmaster General in the Senate, which is contrary to common sense, and against the best interests of the people, surely my resolution ought to be adopted, because of all ministers the Postmaster General should, on occasion, be able to appear before the House of Commons and give those explanations which are required of him. Now, he has not only the administration of the post offices in his purview. A few years ago we adopted rural mail delivery, and I claim some credit for that reform, Mr. Speaker. It was under our Government that the system of rural mail delivery was established in this country, and it has created a revolution in rural Canada, having brought the farmer closer to the city and more in contact with the markets than heretofore. In the organization of rural mail delivery, naturally the electors will call upon their representatives to explain why one route was selected in preference to another. And we know, also, that the revision of the mail contracts makes for an enormous pile of correspondence with members of the House of Commons. Therefore, not only as regards the Postmaster General, hut so far as the Minister of the Interior, and the Minister of Labour are concerned, I think that my resolution fully applies and meets the case.
I do not wish, Mr. Speaker, to make this a party resolution. I am speaking as an old parliamentarian, very anxious to expedite and facilitate the business of the House, and I believe that my resolution can be construed as having only that object in view. But speaking about the Postmaster General, does it not strike you, Sir, that the Government is somewhat in the wrong? Obviously so. The Postmaster General was a candidate at the last general election in two constituencies: he stood for election in Champlain and also in Laurier-Outremont. In both constituencies he was defeated, horse, foot and artillery. He was defeated hopelessly, but the Government waited for a few months and then appointed him to the other House. The minister did not even resign; he remained in office, and finally, on the eve of a session, the Government, against all British precedent, and against all parliamentary tradition, appointed him to the Senate. Let us draw a contrast between the British system of Government, and the Canadian Tory system. In England, the other day, the Secretary for Agriculture, Sir 
Arthur Griffith-Boscawen, was defeated, and defeated largely on a Canadian issue. He was a member of the Government and ran in the constituency of Dudley, where he was defeated. Do you think the Right Hon. Mr. Lloyd George would take upon himself to appoint Sir Griffith-Boscawen to the House of Lords? No, because there would be a revolt in public opinion if that were done in England. Sir Griffith-Boscawen will run in another constituency, and the whips of the Unionist party in England are at present looking for a riding where he may run as a candidate with a view to becoming Secretary for Agricul ture. I have just read this despatch in on< of the papers:

cttered to resign as member of Parliament for of Taunton, in order to give Sir Arthur Griffith-Boscawen, the recently appoint-ec Minister of Agriculture, who lost the byelection in Dudley, another opportunity to find a seat.
It seems to me that another opportunity should be given to the present Postmaster General to be elected by his peers. My right hon. friend would probably say: Well, they appoint ministers of the Crown in England, to the House of Lords. Yes, they do. 1 notice in this morning's papers that a peerage has been offered to Mr. Bonar Law, but he has declined it. I can understand that a gentleman who has served his country brilliantly and with distinction, as he did for several years, may be offered, as in the case of Mr. Morley, a seat in the House of Lords. There can be no objection to his taking that honour. But, generally a public man does not take it with a cabinet portfolio. If he does, it is exceptional, and the department over which he presides is not an important one which would come under the everyday survey of the House of Commons.
I expressed the hope that my right hon. friend, who I know is British at heart, having at least said so during the last elections, and, indeed, having always lived up to British ideals, will in this matter maintain British tradition. I appeal to him and say: Be British! Here is a concrete case in which you have an opportunity to show your love of British tradition. You have the county of Yamaska, where my hon. friend, the present Postmaster General was born and brought up. Thai constituency is open at the present time, and there is a chance for him to appear before his peers, and get a mandate from the people. However, as I said a moment ago, this is not a party resolution; this

suggestion is only an aside, and I say it in all candour. I should like the members of the House on both sides to consider the feasibility of the application of my proposal. I move the resolution because I believe that, if adopted, it will facilitate and expedite the business of the House. It will demonstrate that the Government has some regard for the popular chamber. Above all, if the resolution is adopted, it will be an object lesson that in Canada we are in accord with the principles of responsible Government; and it is above all on that principle of responsible Government that I appeal to the House and ask it to support my resolution.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: THE HOUSING PROBLEM. PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF A FEDERAL HOUSING BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when
I first observed this resolution on the Order Paper it struck me as one of the most interesting and striking suggestions that I had seen on that paper for many years. At the time I had not heard that a change in our system had previously been suggested. But on referring to the records of both Houses for years gone by, I found a discussion of the same question taking place in the upper chamber in 1908. At that time the Government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier was in office. I am not aware how many ministers of that Government sat in the upper chamber, but not less, I believe, than two; and it was a matter of comment that so few ministers found their seats in the upper chamber, and a matter for a very general expression of regret, particularly in that chamber itself.
My hon. friend in urging this motion assumes, by way partly of an aside, that there are too many ministers of the present Government in the Senate, and particularly those who are at the head of the departments that should be especially responsible to, and in intimate association with, the House of Commons. I know that an argument to that end is not to the purpose of the resolution, but it might be worth while to refer to his contention in this regard for a moment. It is noteworthy that in the debate that took place in the Senate in 1908, a resolution was moved by a supporter of the Administration of that time, the Hon. Mr. David, a supporter indeed of the same party to-day, and in that resolution he expressed regret at the smallness of the number of ministers in the upper chamber. The resolution then proposed by Hon. Mr. David was as follows:
That the Senate, while not desiring to pronounce finally upon the numerous and various projects of reform which have been proposed
and discussed in connection with the Senate, yet in view of the differences of opinion on this subject, and until these projects have had time to mature, believes it opportune to declare that it is desirable in order to increase the efficiency of the Senate, that more legislation be initiated in the House, that more ministers of the Crown have seats therein, and that any minister personally may introduce and defend Government measures in both Houses.
That was moved by way of amendment to a resolution of the Hon. Mr. McMullen, and a further amendment was moved to this resolution. A debate ensued, but it
9 p.m. must be admitted that the discussion of the proposal brought forward was by no means so thorough or so interesting as that which the hon. member has been able to present to-night. Anyway, the reference I have made indicates that there was manifest at the time, and the debate shows it pretty definitely, a regret that there were not more of the ministers of the Crown in the upper chamber, and that more legislation did not initiate there. Nor was there any comment, in the course of that debate, on the subject of the special portfolios that might be held by ministers who had their seats there.
I followed closely the argument of the hon. member. He contended, with much emphasis, that it was unfair to Parliament that ministers of* important departments, and particularly spending departments, should have their seats in the Senate and not in the House of Commons; but my perception must be wrong if there was anything in the argument which he presented that would not apply to the minister of any department in the service of the Crown.
Every department is a spending department-some, of course, much more so than others. The largest spending departments are by no means the three that now are served by ministers in the upper chamber; but in so far as the spending of money is concerned that all comes before the Commons and the Commons alone. The Commons and the Commons alone must vote each and every individual item; and there-fpre, in that regard the power of consideration and criticism is vested in this assembly and its opportunity for that is ample. From that standpoint I am not able to appreciate the difference between the wisdom of having a minister at the head of a department sitting in the Senate and of having a minister sitting here-the difference between a minister sitting here and the minister of another department sitting in the other House. I know not what department may be chosen to which the argument of the hon. gentleman would not, in the main, apply. If

we take for example, the Department of the Secretary of State and the Department of the Minister of Justice; these are not great spending departments, but they are large and important ones. They are departments having to do with the administration of affairs of vital and prominent concern, affairs in respect of which the representatives of the people must be in close and intimate touch from day to day; and there is no argument the hon. member has presented against the Postmaster General being a _ member of the upper house, that would not equally apply to show that the Secretary of State, or that the Minister of Justice, should not be a member of that House.

speechtext: What about the Solicitor General?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: THE HOUSING PROBLEM. PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF A FEDERAL HOUSING BOARD
speechtext:
The Solicitor General is not in the Commons a duplicate Minister of Justice. The Solicitor General, at all events since I occupied the office, has functions and duties in which, in no sense, does he review or come into direct contact with the work of the Minister of Justice himself. He takes a special line of work. I know what it is. That work he discharges; but that does not bring him into contact with the work discharged by the Minister of Justice nor with the superintendence of the various services over which the Minister of Justice presides. It seems to me that, while we have the bicameral system, there must be a number of ministers in the upper chamber, or the upper chamber cannot serve even that share of the public duties which it now serves; minor, I must say, in very many respects to those served by this chamber; it cannot serve even those, if we are ever still further to reduce the representation of the Government in that House. The hon. member argues, and argues well, that the bi-cameral system has many supporters in this country, has a very large proportion of public opinion behind it, and argues still more forcibly that whatever that proportion may be, it is very likely to continue in this country, in some form, for many years and decades to come. It is rooted in considerations that go to the protection of minorities -considerations that are particularly applicable to conditions in this Dominion. Consequently, though its functions may not be as important as was antieinated by the Fathers of Confederation, nevertheless it is bound for many years to come to remain one of the three estates of this country.
Coming to the real logic of the resolution, it seeks to have this House affirm that

ministers of the Crown in this chamber should have the right to pass to the other chamber '"whenever measures and policies are introduced affecting their respective departments" and speak thereon, and, similarly, that ministers of the Crown in the other chamber should, under like conditions, come here and enjoy the same privilege. I must say that much for which the hon. gentleman contends appeals to me, and I can see a very great deal of advantage indeed in such a system as he urges. On the other hand, there is very much to be considered before we launch definitely on any such scheme. One point was raised by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean). For example, if a minister of the Crown in the Senate is to be allowed to come to the Commons to speak in relation, say, to his own Estimates, but not to make a motion or to vote, he virtually cannot conduct his Estimates through this House at all, because every discussion in the passage of Estimates arises on a motion, express or implied, that a certain vote appearing in the Estimates be made by this House. He cannot make that motion, consequently it must be assumed to be made by some one else. He is here to discuss it. But many discussions arise in this chamber where it would be very difficult to decide just whether it affected sufficiently the department over which presides the minister having a seat in the Senate to warrant that minister coming into this House and taking part in the debate. I presume it would be for the Speaker to decide just what the relationship was between the discussion and that department. But it would seem to me that if you go a certain length you must go all the way. and you must admit that a minister in either House can speak in the other House in relation to any subject that he desires to discuss. I think there would be very many practical difficulties in drawing a line and saying, "On subiects within a certain line you may come into the other House and address the Chair and the members thereof; but upon subjects beyond that line you must stay where you are." Anyway, I do not know that there would be very much to be feared if a minister were permitted to come into this House from the Senate and discuss any topic that is before us; or, vice versa, that a minister might go from this House to the Senate and discuss any topic that is under discussion there. In practice it would be availed of only in such cases as seemed to call for the attention of the minister in question in the other House. Very likely it

would work out in that way and there would be very little abuse of the privilege.
There is, though, this point that 1 should like to raise. The resolution, of course, only affirms a principle and does not in any way indicate how it is to be carried out. It would occur to me questionable indeed, whether this House or the upper house could, by its own resolution alone, enable one of its members to come into the other House and to take part in its proceedings as is intended by this resolution. Is it within the power of this House of Commons by resolution to enable a member of the Upper House to come and take his seat among us and to exercise in debate his influence upon the votes and decisions of this assembly? If that is to be done, must it not be done by amendment to the constitution itself? And if that is the proper procedure, then an Address from both Houses to the British Parliament would of course be the appropriate action leading to that end. It was suggested in the debate in 1908, I think by the Speaker of the Senate at that time, that there was power in either assembly by resolution to give this right to ministers sitting in the other House. But no argument was presented in favour of that contention, and its mere assertion did not appeal to me as sound. Anyway, I apprehend that neither this House nor the other House is going to take a step so important as this-because it is a very important step-after only one discussion, however thorough. It is naturally a question that should be debated not only in the two Houses of Parliament, but by the people, through the press, before we launch upon such a course. The debate which we have had will serve the purpose of bringing the question before the people, and I for one am very glad indeed that this resolution has been introduced by the hon. member who has just taken his seat, for he is well qualified from his historic knowledge and his parliamentary experience to debate the subject with profit to us all.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think that probably the House will be disposed to agree with the right hon. the leader of the Government (Mr. Meighen) in his view that the House could hardly be expected to adopt the resolution at the present time; and I fancy that that was scarcely the intention of the mover of it. To a certain extent I am disposed to agree with the principle enunciated in the resolution, that members of the House of Commons who are members of the Government should be permitted to go to the Senate and there take the direction and control of measures which originate in this House. Speaking generally, it has in the past, I think, been the practice to have but one representative of the Government in the Senate. It is true that on certain occasions there have been two or more, and at the present time there are three members of the Government sitting in the upper chamber. I remember, however, when for a considerable time there was but one minister sitting in the Senate, and that was the leader of the Senate, Sir James Lougheed. The practice of having as few members of the Government as possible holding seats in the Senate has always been adhered to, and I think it reflects the spirit of our Constitution. Support of this view will be found in the fact that during our whole history the major portion of every ministry have been members of the House of Commons. That practice is true of the British Parliament as well. There are very many reasons why this practice should prevail, but it is not my intention to detain the House in discussing them.
Coming back to my statement of a moment ago, that ordinarily but one or two members of our Governments have held seats in the Senate, that is easily accounted for by the fact that there would be but one minister available there for actual work, as has occurred on many occasions. It is utterly impossible-perhaps I should say unfair-to expect one member of the Government to handle in the Senate all the Government business originating in this House. I remember when the whole direction of Government business in the Senate was entirely in the hands of Sir James Lougheed, the present Government leader in the Senate. It was a marvel that he was able to take care of that large volume of work and those numerous parliamentary duties as he did, in such a very excellent manner. I think it is hardly fair to Parliament or to the country that such a vast amount of business should be laid upon the shoulders of one person. Should there be but one member of the Government in the Senate it is not difficult to imagine that on occasions he might be ill or incapacitated for one or more reasons and unable to handle Government legislation. It does seem to me, therefore, that it is quite a rational suggestion that members	of	this House who aremembers	of	the Government should
have the privilege of going to the Senate and there taking direction or control of

Government legislation, or at least assisting the Senate in the consideration of it. For that reason I would think that such a proposed amendment as is incorporated in the resolution of the hon. member from Maisonneuve is a rational one and in the public interest, and to that extent I desire to express my hearty approval of it.
Now, it may be asked if I approve the resolution to that extent, why should I not go further and say that members of the Government holding seats in the Senate * should be enabled to come to this Chamber. Well, I think if that were permitted, abuses might very easily creep into our parliamentary practice. For instance, if a government were very weak it might have the major portion of its membership in the Senate, Contrary to the spirit of the constitution and probably against the wishes of the people. That, I think, would be one serious objection. Then, the reasons in favour of the suggestion that senators who are members of the Government should come to this Chamber do not apply to the proposal that members of the Government sitting in this Chamber should go to the Senate. There usually are sufficient members of the Government in this Chamber to handle expeditiously the Government business or the public business, whereas, as I have pointed out, that condition might not always prevail in the Senate. So that the reason for my suggestion is stronger than the reason that may be advanced for the broader suggestion contained in the resolution.
I am not disposed to agree with the suggestion made by Mr. McMullen, a former member of the Senate, referred to by the right hon. leader of the House, to the effect that there was not sufficient representation in the Senate of members of the Govern-merit. I do not know that we can ever get much enlightenment from former debates on any abstract resolution. It might happen that a Government would be in the minority in the Senate and I doubt very much whether the Senate would be bound to respect Government legislation introduced by a member of the Government in a body where his party or his Government did not hold a majority, as they would be bound, I think, to respect legislation coming from the popular chamber where the Government was supported by a popular majority. I think upon this ground one might urge very substantial objection to the suggestion which was made in the Senate in 1908 as indicated by the extract from the Senate proceedings just read to the House by the Prime Minister.

I have nothing further to say, Mr. Speaker, except to repeat in a word, what I have already said: that the suggestion that members of this House who are members of the Government be permitted to go to the Senate is eminently a proper and a rational one, and I trust that at some time in the early future an amendment to our parliamentary practice will be made or the necessary steps taken to enable that to be done. On the other hand, I do not think that reasons so strong can be advanced for permitting members of the Senate who are members of the Government to come to this Chamber.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) :
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: THE HOUSING PROBLEM. PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF A FEDERAL HOUSING BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not rise to express a settled opinion upon the proposal that has been made. It is certainly a most interesting one, and while I would be prepared to concur in the view that practical advantages might result from its being carried out, I think it is one which calls for careful consideration before arriving at a final decision and, above all, before taking action.
There is one phase of the matter to which I would like to direct the attention of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lemieux) who made the motion, and the attention of the House generally. It seems to me that the proposal involves a fundamental change in our system of government and, really, in the British Constitution. Our parliamentary system is based upon the conception of the existence of two distinct bodies deriving their authority, if I may use that word-their right of action, from two totally different sources. We have the peoples' Chamber, and. then we have the other Chamber which does not derive its authority directly from the people, which under our system is composed of nominees of the Crown, and which under the original British system was composed largely of representatives of a particular class of the people who sat there because they belonged to that class. Now, resulting from the different sources from which these two bodies derive their authority, there has grown up a system under which particular things belong specially to these two bodies. Take, for instance, everything that touches the voting of money; that belongs to the popular Chamber. It has been suggested that there would be advantages in a minister, being a member of the Senate, coming into this House and discussing his Estimates. What quality would he, as a member of the Senate, have in the discussion of the moneys that the people's representatives

ought to vote? Is it not consistent with the spirit of our Constitution that the people's representatives should act absolutely independently of any other influence when they are dealing with matters of that kind, matters which pertain specially to them; matters in regard to which it is for. the people through their chosen representatives to speak? It may be said that it is not suggested that that member of the Senate should vote. So far, so good; but the deliberation is, I think, at least as important as the vote. Can you conceive of this popular assembly being guided, in a matter pertaining to the voting of the people's money, by a gentleman who is not a representative of the people at all, a gentleman whose role in the parliamentary work of this country is to be and act as a member of a body, constituted, after all, to exercise a species of supervising and, perhaps it might not be a mistake to say, moderating influence upon the actions of this chamber? On the other hand is it proper that into the deliberations of this body constituted for the purpose of exercising that supervising and moderating influence, a body which in consequence, ought to approach the measures that come to it from this assembly in a-I do not think it would be a mistake to say-quasi-judicial frame of mind, there should be interjected a member or members of this House whose action, in a general sort of way, those who are responsible for the constitution, thought it desirable should be submitted to the reconsideration of a body not so directly, as this body is, under the immediate influence of the popular feeling of the moment. I do not say that these reasons are, perhaps, conclusive against this proposal, or some proposal along these lines, being adopted at some time. - But I would invite the House to consider these things that I have pointed out, and to realize that if, in its wisdom, it should decide that it is desirable to recommend a change of this kind, it is recommending a very fundamental change. If this proposal is adopted,
. we shall have a new system of parliamentary government. We shall have brought into combination two bodies which, up to the present time, the constitution has looked upon as absolutely distinct bodies called upon to exercise absolutely distinct functions, the one to be the immediate or direct mouthpiece of the people of the country, the other, a body that may serve, when need may be for that, because such things happen, as a species of moderating, super-74
vising body, a body which, therefore, should approach matters with which it is called upon to deal, in the frame of mind that belongs to people who are taking up the action of others, to consider whether it was wise or not.
I, perhaps, may stop there because my purpose really is only to call attention to what seems to me to be the very fundamental nature of the proposal. But looking at it from a practical point of view, might we not have very undesirable situations created, if you have a member of this House taking part in the deliberations of the supervising body and, perhaps, feeling himself called upon to act as a sort of advocate for this House of Commons? It does not seem to me that that would be a desirable situation. I am not quite sure that it would be conducive to the perfect free play of the functions of the two bodies or to the maintenance and preservation of the harmony, whether they agree with regard to particular measures or not, that it is certainly most desirable, should be preserved between the two bodies. I would earnestly invite the House, before coming to a conclusion upon this matter, to give most serious thought to just what is involved in the change that is proposed.,
